script.opening: (Mia, tired, pale, sitting propped on cushions; mother beside her.) "Every time I stand up I go dizzy, my heart pounds and races, and I get this fog where I can't think. Sometimes I nearly faint. It's wrecking school — I keep having to sit down or go home, and I heard a teacher say I'm just attention-seeking. I'm not making it up. Mum had to push to get me seen."

facts.text: "I'm not sure exactly. It's been getting worse" — about 5 months, started a few weeks after a bad flu-like illness.

Within a minute or two of standing, and worse standing still in queues, in hot showers and after big meals. "Yes. Lying down, it goes." Heart races ("like after running"). Shaky, sweaty, nauseous. Brain fog and headaches.
"I've never fully blacked out. Not during PE — I just feel awful when I stand still." No collapse during exercise, no chest pain, no palpitations lying down, no fits, no injury.
If asked about sudden deaths or heart problems: (Mum) "Not that we know of."
"I don't drink loads, to be honest. Eating's okay. Periods are normal, I think" — about 1 litre a day, mostly squash; not heavy periods. No weight loss. No vomiting or bingeing.
"No" — no medicines, no allergies, no recreational drugs or energy drinks. Joint hypermobility — "I can bend my thumb back to my wrist." No previous health problems.
Year 12, doing A-levels. Attendance dropped to 70%. Stopped netball. Sleeps 10 hours and still tired.

"I feel rubbish about it. I'm tired all the time. I worry people think I'm faking." Low at times but no thoughts of self-harm. If offered time alone: nothing extra to disclose, but grateful to be asked.
Can lie on the sofa and then stand while Mum counts her pulse if the doctor suggests — pulse goes from about 72 to "over 120" — but it's hard to be accurate.

Exhausted and wary of not being believed. Engages warmly if the doctor talks to her directly. If the doctor says it's probably anxiety without investigating, she goes quiet and Mum objects. Relieved: "So I'm not making it up." Practical: "I can do the water thing." (Mum) A school letter "would make a huge difference".

ice.ideas: "Something's wrong with how my body handles standing."
ice.concerns: Being called a faker; missing school during A-levels; exhaustion; not knowing what it is.
ice.expectations: "I want someone to believe me and to tell school."

cues: "I'm not making it up." — needs to be believed.
"A teacher said I'm attention-seeking." — school impact to act on.

checkpoints.text: Takes the teenager’s disabling symptoms SERIOUSLY and does NOT default to "anxiety/attention-seeking" — recognising anxiety may coexist but is not a substitute for assessment

Recognises the PoTS picture (orthostatic dizziness/palpitations/brain fog/near-syncope on standing with a sustained HR rise ≥40 bpm at her age (≥30 in adults; HRS 2015, international) and no significant BP drop) and assesses for it specifically

Works the DIFFERENTIAL — postural hypotension, vasovagal syncope, anaemia, thyroid, arrhythmia/inherited cardiac disease (screening exertional/lying syncope, palpitations, FAMILY HISTORY of sudden death), hypoglycaemia, medication, anxiety

Arranges an ACTIVE STANDING test face to face (lying/standing HR and BP — not possible over video) and basic tests (FBC, ferritin, U&E, TFTs, glucose, ECG), and refers to cardiology for NICE CG109 red flags

Gives NON-DRUG-FIRST PoTS management (increased fluid and salt — amounts agreed with the specialist for a teenager, as the 2–3 L figure is adult — gradual position change, compression, graded reconditioning, trigger avoidance) and knows medication is specialist-initiated; refers to PoTS/cardiology/paediatrics as appropriate

BELIEVES and engages the teenager DIRECTLY, validates the very real school/functional and psychological impact, and advocates concretely (letter, individual healthcare plan under the Children and Families Act 2014 s100, reasonable adjustments), offering time alone and confidentiality at 16, rather than dismissing her
Explains PoTS and the plan in accessible terms, addresses any coexisting anxiety supportively without using it to dismiss, and checks understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: cardiac red flags warranting urgent review, results and referral, school liaison/adjustments, management plan with review, and support for the functional/psychological impact — a proper work-up, not dismissal as attention-seeking

worked.txt: (To Mia directly.) "I want to say this clearly: I believe you, and what you’re describing is real — it is NOT attention-seeking. Standing up shouldn’t make you feel like that, and I’m going to take it seriously and work out why."

"There’s a condition that fits this really well — PoTS — where, when you stand, your heart races too much and you get dizzy, foggy and exhausted, even though your blood pressure mostly holds. It’s common in young women and it’s genuinely disabling, not in your head."

"Let me check it properly: I can’t do this over video, so I’d like you to come in so we can measure your heart rate and blood pressure lying down and then standing for up to ten minutes. I’ll also do some bloods — your iron and thyroid — and a heart tracing. Quick question: do you ever faint during exercise, or has anyone in the family died suddenly young?"

"A lot of the treatment is things you control: drinking plenty through the day — the specialist will help set the right amount for you — more salt in your diet, standing up slowly, compression socks, and gradually building up exercise. These genuinely help. If needed, the specialists can add medication."

"School absolutely should not be calling this attention-seeking. I’ll write a letter explaining it’s a real medical condition and ask for adjustments — water at your desk, being allowed to sit, rest breaks, flexibility around exams. Schools have a legal duty to support pupils with medical conditions, usually with a healthcare plan. You shouldn’t have to fight to be believed."

"This has clearly worn you down, and it’s okay if it’s affected your mood too — we can support that as well, alongside, not instead of. If you faint without warning, faint during exercise, or get chest pain, tell us urgently. I’ll refer you and we’ll review with the results."

f.learning: Disabling postural symptoms in a teenager must be taken SERIOUSLY and worked up — defaulting to "it’s just anxiety/attention-seeking" (as the school here has) is both a clinical error and damaging; anxiety may coexist or contribute but is not a substitute for assessment. Recognise the POSTURAL TACHYCARDIA SYNDROME (PoTS) picture: orthostatic symptoms (dizziness, palpitations, brain fog, fatigue, near-syncope) on standing, with a sustained heart-rate rise of ≥30 bpm (≥40 bpm at ages 12–19) within 10 minutes of standing and WITHOUT a significant postural BP drop (Heart Rhythm Society 2015, international) — commoner in young women, often post-viral or with hypermobility, and genuinely disabling. Work the differential (postural hypotension, vasovagal syncope, anaemia/iron deficiency, thyroid disease, and the must-not-miss arrhythmia/inherited cardiac disease — screen the NICE CG109 red flags (exertional syncope, FAMILY HISTORY of sudden cardiac death under 40 or inherited cardiac condition, abnormal ECG, heart failure, unexplained breathlessness, murmur) plus lying syncope and palpitations with collapse — plus hypoglycaemia, medication and anxiety). Assess with an ACTIVE STANDING test arranged face to face (lying/standing HR and BP at intervals — not possible over video) and basic tests (FBC, ferritin, U&E, TFTs, glucose, ECG), referring to cardiology for red flags. PoTS management is NON-DRUG-FIRST (HRS 2015, international) — increased fluid (the 2–3 L/day figure is for adults; agree a teenager’s amount with the specialist) and salt, gradual position change, physical counter-manoeuvres, compression garments, graded reconditioning exercise, sleep and trigger avoidance — with specialist-initiated medication if needed. Crucially, BELIEVE and engage the teenager directly, VALIDATE the real school/functional and psychological impact, and ADVOCATE concretely (a letter and reasonable adjustments — water, seating, rest, exam flexibility — with the school’s duty under the Children and Families Act 2014 s100, usually an individual healthcare plan), offering her time alone and confidentiality at 16 (GMC 0–18 years), addressing any coexisting anxiety supportively without using it to dismiss her, and refer appropriately.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE CG109 (transient loss of consciousness in over-16s) · [2] Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement on POTS, 2015 (international) · [3] NICE NG136 (postural BP measurement, updated 2026) · [4] Children and Families Act 2014 s100 and DfE Supporting pupils at school with medical conditions (2015) · [5] Equality Act 2010 · [6] GMC 0–18 years (2018)
knowledge.summary: Standing-triggered dizziness, palpitations and brain fog that settle on lying down deserve a proper work-up. Exclude cardiac and other causes, do an active stand test, and if PoTS is likely, start non-drug measures and advocate for her at school. Anxiety may coexist, but it is never a default diagnosis.

points.t: HRS 2015 [2] (international): frequent orthostatic symptoms with a sustained heart-rate rise of ≥30 bpm (≥40 bpm at ages 12–19) within 10 minutes of standing, without orthostatic hypotension, and without another cause of sinus tachycardia. Commoner in young women; may follow a viral illness.

Vasovagal syncope, orthostatic hypotension, dehydration or poor intake, anaemia or iron deficiency (ask about periods), thyroid disease, medicines, eating disorder, and — must not miss — arrhythmia or structural or inherited cardiac disease. Anxiety can coexist or amplify symptoms.

NICE CG109 [1] (applies from 16): urgent specialist cardiovascular assessment for an ECG abnormality, heart failure, loss of consciousness during exertion, family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 or an inherited cardiac condition, new or unexplained breathlessness, or a heart murmur. Also ask about collapse while lying down and palpitations before collapse.

Face to face: heart rate and BP after lying for several minutes, then at intervals over 10 minutes of standing [2]. A systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more suggests orthostatic hypotension (NICE NG136 [3]); a sustained HR rise of 40 or more without a BP fall fits PoTS at her age. Cannot be done reliably over video.
12-lead ECG (rhythm, QT, pre-excitation, conduction), FBC, ferritin, U&E, glucose and TFTs. Refer to a specialist syncope, cardiology or autonomic service for diagnostic confirmation where suspected.

HRS 2015 [2] (international): generous fluid intake (2–3 L a day is suggested for adults) and increased salt unless contraindicated — agree amounts with the specialist for a teenager; rise slowly; avoid prolonged standing, heat and large carbohydrate meals; counter-manoeuvres; compression garments; graded, initially recumbent exercise. Medicines (e.g. ivabradine, fludrocortisone, midodrine, beta-blocker) are specialist-initiated and often off-label.

Children and Families Act 2014 s100 [4]: schools must support pupils with medical conditions, usually through an individual healthcare plan. If her condition has a substantial, long-term effect on daily activities, the Equality Act 2010 [5] requires reasonable adjustments. Exam access arrangements can be requested through the school.
GMC 0–18 years [6]: at 16 she is presumed to have capacity to consent. Speak to her directly, offer time alone, and respect her confidentiality while involving her mother with her agreement.

model.text: Hello Mia, and hello Mum. I’m Dr Rahman. Mia, I’d like to hear it from you first — what’s been happening?

Every time I stand up I go dizzy, my heart pounds and races, and I get this fog where I can’t think. Sometimes I nearly faint. It’s wrecking school — I heard a teacher say I’m attention-seeking. I’m not making it up. Mum had to push to get me seen.

Thank you, Mia. I want to say clearly: I believe you. What you’re describing is real, and I’m going to take it seriously. I’ll ask some questions, explain what I think, and we’ll make a plan together — including school. Is that okay with you both?
model.why: Believes her explicitly and sets a shared agenda

model.text: Yes. Thank you.
When did this start, and was there anything around then — an illness, a virus?
I’m not sure exactly. It’s been getting worse.
Does it happen only when you’re upright, and settle when you sit or lie down?
Yes. Lying down, it goes.
Have you ever actually passed out? And has it ever happened while you’re exercising, or while you’re lying down?
model.why: Screens for exertional or supine syncope — cardiac red flags

model.text: I’ve never fully blacked out. Not during PE — I just feel awful when I stand still.
Any chest pain, or getting breathless more than your friends?
No.
Mum, maybe you know this best: has anyone in the family died suddenly or unexpectedly young, or had a heart condition that runs in families?
model.why: Family history of sudden cardiac death or inherited cardiac disease

model.text: (Mum) Not that we know of.
Mia, a few more: how much do you drink in a day, how’s your eating, and are your periods heavy?
model.why: Screens dehydration, eating disorder and iron-deficiency risk

model.text: I don’t drink loads, to be honest. Eating’s okay. Periods are normal, I think.
Thanks. Mum, would it be okay if I spoke to Mia on her own for a minute? It’s something I do with everyone her age.
model.why: Offers confidential time alone, as for any 16-year-old

model.text: (Mum) Of course.
Mia, just us now. How is all this affecting you — your mood, sleep, friends?
I feel rubbish about it. I’m tired all the time. I worry people think I’m faking.
That sounds really hard, and it’s okay if it gets you down. It doesn’t mean it’s ‘just anxiety’. What do you think is going on, and what were you hoping we’d do today?
model.why: Elicits ideas and expectations without dismissing

model.text: Something’s wrong with how my body handles standing. I want someone to believe me and to tell school.

(Mum back.) You might be right, Mia. There’s a condition called PoTS — postural tachycardia syndrome — where standing makes the heart race too much and you feel dizzy, foggy and exhausted, even though the blood pressure mostly holds. It’s real, it’s commoner in young women, and it can be managed.
model.why: Explains the likely diagnosis in plain words

model.text: So I’m not making it up.

Definitely not. But I need to check properly and rule out other causes. I’d like you in the surgery for a standing test — we measure your heart rate and blood pressure lying down, then standing for ten minutes. Plus a heart tracing and blood tests for iron, blood count, thyroid, kidneys and sugar.
model.why: Active stand test, ECG and baseline bloods face to face

model.text: Okay.

Meanwhile, there are things that genuinely help: drinking more through the day, standing up slowly, not standing still for long, crossing your legs or clenching your calves when you feel it coming, and avoiding hot showers and big sugary meals. We’ll discuss extra salt and compression tights once the tests are back.
model.why: Starts safe non-drug measures while tests are pending

model.text: I can do the water thing.

And school. I’ll write a letter saying this is a medical problem being investigated, asking for water in class, being allowed to sit, rest breaks and an individual healthcare plan. Schools have a legal duty to support pupils with medical conditions. We can ask about exam arrangements too.
(Mum) That would make a huge difference.
If the tests fit PoTS, I’ll refer you to a specialist team who can confirm it and add medicine if needed. Mia, can you tell me what we’ve agreed, in your own words?
Standing test and bloods and a heart tracing. Drink more, stand up slowly. A letter for school. Then maybe a specialist.

Perfect. Some things need urgent help: fainting during exercise, fainting while lying down, chest pain, or palpitations followed by collapse — that’s 999 or A&E. If you fully faint for any reason, contact us the same day. I’ll see you with the results. Anything else?
model.why: Specific cardiac red flags and follow-up

model.text: No. Thank you for believing me.
You shouldn’t have had to fight for it. We’ll sort this out together.

social.t: Missed school and exam worries. A school letter, an individual healthcare plan and exam access arrangements reduce the harm.
Her mother advocated to get her seen; involve her with Mia’s agreement.

legal.t: Schools must make arrangements to support pupils with medical conditions (DfE statutory guidance, 2015).
If the condition has a substantial and long-term effect on daily activities, it can count as a disability, and reasonable adjustments are required.
Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies from 16: presume capacity. GMC 0–18 years (2018): offer confidential time alone.

professional.t: GMC 0–18 years: listen to children and young people and take their views seriously.
Coexisting anxiety should not stop assessment for physical causes.

community.t: PoTS UK (charity) information for patients, families and schools; school nurse involvement.

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you take a young person seriously while still thinking clinically. It is failed by dismissal, by missing cardiac red flags, and by ignoring the school problem she came about.

items.why: Mia is 16 and the patient; talking over her repeats the experience of not being heard.
items.fix: Ask Mia first, and offer time alone.

items.fail: Diagnosing anxiety on the history alone.
items.why: Diagnostic overshadowing; physical causes, including cardiac ones, are missed.
items.fix: Screen cardiac red flags, plan an active stand, ECG and bloods, and treat anxiety as a possible contributor.

items.fail: No family history of sudden death or exertional syncope.
items.why: These are NICE CG109 red flags for urgent cardiology.
items.fix: Ask both explicitly, and ask Mum about the family history.

items.why: HR and BP over 10 minutes need proper equipment and supervision.
items.fix: Book a face-to-face appointment for the stand test and ECG.

items.fail: Starting a beta-blocker or fludrocortisone in primary care.
items.why: PoTS drugs are specialist-initiated and often off-label.
It is her main reason for attending; ignoring it scores poorly.
items.fix: Offer a letter, an individual healthcare plan and exam arrangements.

SCA_STEM.recent: Recurrent light-headedness, palpitations, ‘brain fog’ and near-faints on standing, easing on sitting or lying. Missing school. Mother present.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation, booked by her mother: “Every time I stand up I go dizzy — school think I’m making it up.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE CG109 (transient loss of consciousness in over-16s) · [2] Heart Rhythm Society expert consensus statement on POTS, 2015 (international) · [3] NICE NG136 (postural BP measurement, updated 2026) · [4] Children and Families Act 2014 s100 and DfE Supporting pupils at school with medical conditions (2015) · [5] Equality Act 2010 · [6] GMC 0–18 years (2018)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Standing-triggered dizziness, palpitations and brain fog that settle on lying down deserve a proper work-up. Exclude cardiac and other causes, do an active stand test, and if PoTS is likely, start non-drug measures and advocate for her at school. Anxiety may coexist, but it is never a default diagnosis.

points.t: HRS 2015 [2] (international): frequent orthostatic symptoms with a sustained heart-rate rise of ≥30 bpm (≥40 bpm at ages 12–19) within 10 minutes of standing, without orthostatic hypotension, and without another cause of sinus tachycardia. Commoner in young women; may follow a viral illness.

Vasovagal syncope, orthostatic hypotension, dehydration or poor intake, anaemia or iron deficiency (ask about periods), thyroid disease, medicines, eating disorder, and — must not miss — arrhythmia or structural or inherited cardiac disease. Anxiety can coexist or amplify symptoms.

NICE CG109 [1] (applies from 16): urgent specialist cardiovascular assessment for an ECG abnormality, heart failure, loss of consciousness during exertion, family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 or an inherited cardiac condition, new or unexplained breathlessness, or a heart murmur. Also ask about collapse while lying down and palpitations before collapse.

Face to face: heart rate and BP after lying for several minutes, then at intervals over 10 minutes of standing [2]. A systolic fall of 20 mmHg or more suggests orthostatic hypotension (NICE NG136 [3]); a sustained HR rise of 40 or more without a BP fall fits PoTS at her age. Cannot be done reliably over video.
12-lead ECG (rhythm, QT, pre-excitation, conduction), FBC, ferritin, U&E, glucose and TFTs. Refer to a specialist syncope, cardiology or autonomic service for diagnostic confirmation where suspected.

HRS 2015 [2] (international): generous fluid intake (2–3 L a day is suggested for adults) and increased salt unless contraindicated — agree amounts with the specialist for a teenager; rise slowly; avoid prolonged standing, heat and large carbohydrate meals; counter-manoeuvres; compression garments; graded, initially recumbent exercise. Medicines (e.g. ivabradine, fludrocortisone, midodrine, beta-blocker) are specialist-initiated and often off-label.

Children and Families Act 2014 s100 [4]: schools must support pupils with medical conditions, usually through an individual healthcare plan. If her condition has a substantial, long-term effect on daily activities, the Equality Act 2010 [5] requires reasonable adjustments. Exam access arrangements can be requested through the school.
GMC 0–18 years [6]: at 16 she is presumed to have capacity to consent. Speak to her directly, offer time alone, and respect her confidentiality while involving her mother with her agreement.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Addressed Mia directly; let her tell the story; explicitly believed her.
Explored school impact, fatigue, mood, eating, fluids, periods; offered time alone.
Picked up ‘attention-seeking’, ‘Mum had to push’ and the fear of not being believed.
Idea: something wrong with how her body handles standing. Concern: being dismissed; school. Expectation: to be believed and school told.
Face-to-face active stand test; ECG; FBC, ferritin, U&E, glucose, TFTs.
PoTS vs vasovagal, orthostatic hypotension, anaemia, thyroid, dehydration, eating disorder, arrhythmia; anxiety as a contributor.
Screened exertional and supine syncope, chest pain, breathlessness, family sudden death (NICE CG109 red flags).
Likely PoTS pending confirmation, explained in plain language without dismissing anxiety’s possible role.
Non-drug measures started; salt and compression after results; specialist referral; medicines specialist-initiated.
Mood and psychological impact explored privately; confidentiality respected (GMC 0–18 years).
School letter and healthcare plan; teach-back; 999 cardiac red flags; review with results.

social.t: Missed school and exam worries. A school letter, an individual healthcare plan and exam access arrangements reduce the harm.
Her mother advocated to get her seen; involve her with Mia’s agreement.

legal.t: Schools must make arrangements to support pupils with medical conditions (DfE statutory guidance, 2015).
If the condition has a substantial and long-term effect on daily activities, it can count as a disability, and reasonable adjustments are required.
Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies from 16: presume capacity. GMC 0–18 years (2018): offer confidential time alone.

professional.t: GMC 0–18 years: listen to children and young people and take their views seriously.
Coexisting anxiety should not stop assessment for physical causes.

community.t: PoTS UK (charity) information for patients, families and schools; school nurse involvement.

redFlags: Syncope during exertion or while lying down — urgent cardiology
Family history of sudden cardiac death under 40 or inherited cardiac condition
Chest pain, palpitations followed by collapse, new breathlessness, abnormal ECG or murmur (NICE CG109)
psychosocial: School absence and being called attention-seeking
ice: Idea: something wrong with how her body copes with standing
Concern: not being believed; school and exams
Expectation: to be believed and for school to be told

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Orthostatic intolerance, probable PoTS, pending active stand test, ECG and bloods; cardiac and other causes still to exclude.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “When you stand, blood pools in your legs. Your heart speeds up a lot to compensate, which causes the racing, dizziness and fog. It’s a real problem with how your body adjusts to standing.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted someone to believe you and to tell school. I believe you, and I’ll write to them.”
management.psychosocial: School letter and healthcare plan; support for low mood alongside, not instead of, the work-up.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face active stand test, ECG, FBC, ferritin, U&E, glucose, TFTs
Non-drug measures now: fluids, rise slowly, counter-manoeuvres, avoid triggers; salt and compression after results
Specialist referral if PoTS likely; medicines specialist-initiated
safetyNet: 999/A&E: fainting during exercise or lying down, chest pain, palpitations then collapse
Same day: any full faint; review with results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you take a young person seriously while still thinking clinically. It is failed by dismissal, by missing cardiac red flags, and by ignoring the school problem she came about.

items.why: Mia is 16 and the patient; talking over her repeats the experience of not being heard.
items.fix: Ask Mia first, and offer time alone.

items.fail: Diagnosing anxiety on the history alone.
items.why: Diagnostic overshadowing; physical causes, including cardiac ones, are missed.
items.fix: Screen cardiac red flags, plan an active stand, ECG and bloods, and treat anxiety as a possible contributor.

items.fail: No family history of sudden death or exertional syncope.
items.why: These are NICE CG109 red flags for urgent cardiology.
items.fix: Ask both explicitly, and ask Mum about the family history.

items.why: HR and BP over 10 minutes need proper equipment and supervision.
items.fix: Book a face-to-face appointment for the stand test and ECG.

items.fail: Starting a beta-blocker or fludrocortisone in primary care.
items.why: PoTS drugs are specialist-initiated and often off-label.
It is her main reason for attending; ignoring it scores poorly.
items.fix: Offer a letter, an individual healthcare plan and exam arrangements.
